Populations & Migrations

How many there were, where — and the movements that carried them from one place to another, in date order

This section keeps the two halves of the record together: the counts — censuses and population figures, tied to the exact country, city or state each source names — and the movements — expulsions, organized transports paid for by men like Baron Hirsch, and journeys people made by their own choice. For every movement, both ends are given wherever the sources give them: the place that sent and the place that received. Where a sending-side figure and an arrival-side figure disagree, both are printed, with their sources, and the difference is noted rather than smoothed over. The companion counts list is The Numbers; the full chronological counts file is the Jewish Population Counts research topic.

The language of the record. This research was done across the press in several languages: English; Yiddish (Der Tog, Der Morgen Zshurnal and the Yidishes Tageblatt in the Library of Congress — the National Library of Israel's Historical Jewish Press stayed blocked on repeated tries, and is recorded as blocked, not as searched); German (the German-American papers of Chronicling America); and Spanish (the Spanish-language papers of the United States). What each language yielded is stated in the sections where it lands.

1492–1497 — Spain expels its Jews; Portugal follows

On March 31, 1492, Ferdinand and Isabella signed the Alhambra Decree: every Jew in Castile and Aragon who would not convert had to leave by the end of July 1492. The last departures were on August 2, 1492.

How many left — the sources disagree, and the range is the honest answer. A contemporary account written in 1495 (preserved in the Fordham Internet Jewish History Sourcebook) gives the generally accepted estimate of his day as 50,000–53,000 families — about 250,000 persons. Modern scholarship is lower and still split: estimates run from 40,000 to 200,000 expelled, out of a Jewish population of perhaps 300,000, with Henry Kamen's tax-based estimate at the low end (about 40,000 emigrated) and older chroniclers at the high end (Isaac Abravanel: 300,000). Many more converted and stayed.

Both ends. The 1495 account counts 120,000 going from Spain into Portugal alone, at one ducat a head. From Portugal and directly from Spain the exiles spread to North Africa (Fez, Tlemcen, the Barbary ports), to Italy (Naples, Rome, Venice, Genoa), and above all to the Ottoman Empire, where Sultan Bayezid II sent ships for them; one modern summary estimates 100,000–150,000 Sephardic Jews settled in Ottoman territories, and by 1519 Jews were more than half the population of Salonica. Portugal then trapped its own refugees: in 1497 King Manuel ordered forced conversion instead of expulsion, and the 1495 account records that 700 children of the Spanish refugees were seized and shipped to the island of São Tomé off Africa.

Sources: Fordham Sourcebook — the 1495 account · Wikipedia — Expulsion of the Jews from Spain

1654 — Recife to New Amsterdam: the 23

When Portugal retook Dutch Brazil in 1654, the Jews of Recife had to leave with the Dutch. One group — 23 people — reached New Amsterdam in September 1654 aboard the St. Charles, by way of the Caribbean. Governor Peter Stuyvesant asked the Dutch West India Company to expel them; the Company refused, and ordered in 1655 that they be allowed to stay. It is the founding arrival of the first Jewish community in North America.

Both ends. Sending side: Recife, Dutch Brazil (with Amsterdam as the deciding authority). Receiving side: New Amsterdam — 23 arrivals, a count the colony's records and later newspaper retellings agree on; the Evening Star of May 21, 1933 retells the arrival of “23 Jews” on the St. Charles in 1654.

Sources: New Amsterdam & the 23 — this site

1669–1670 — Vienna and Austria emptied

Emperor Leopold I ordered the Jews out of Vienna and all Austria. The poorer Jews — some 1,600 — were expelled in the summer of 1669 on two weeks' notice; the rest followed in 1670, deadline August 1, their property taken and the ghetto synagogue destroyed.

How many. The Encyclopaedia Judaica's Vienna entry: the ghetto in 1670 held 136 houses accommodating 500 families, and “of the 3,000–4,000 Jews expelled some made their way to the great cities of Europe.” One modern museum source gives a lower figure, about 1,300 Jews in Vienna at the time — the sources do not agree, and both are shown. Both ends: sending side, Vienna and Austria generally; receiving side, the great cities of Europe and the small towns of Moravia, Bohemia and Hungary — described in general terms, not counts per city, and that one-sidedness is noted honestly.

Sources: Jewish Virtual Library — Vienna · Encyclopaedia Judaica — Vienna

1881–1914 — The Great Migration out of Eastern Europe

The counts before the movement. The Russian Empire's only general census, in 1897, counted 5,215,805 Jews by religion, about 94% of them confined to the Pale of Settlement and Congress Poland. Around 1900, about 9 million Jews lived in Europe out of roughly 10.5–11 million in the world: Austria-Hungary about 2.1 million, Germany 586,948 (1900 census), Romania 269,015, the Netherlands about 106,000, France 86,885.

The movement. After the 1881 pogroms and the May Laws, Jews left Eastern Europe in the largest Jewish migration in history. Sending side: between 1881 and 1914, about 2.5 million Jews left Eastern Europe in all — about 2 million of them from the Russian Empire, about 350,000 from Galicia alone. Samuel Joseph's 1914 Columbia study counted 1,562,800 Jewish entries into the United States in 1881–1910 — 71.6% from the Russian Empire, 17.9% from Austria-Hungary, 4.3% from Romania — with roughly 400,000 more in 1911–1914. The worst single year, both ends itemized: from mid-1905 to mid-1906, more than 200,000 Jews emigrated from Russia — 154,000 to the United States, 13,500 to Argentina, 7,000 to Canada, 3,500 to Palestine, and the remainder to South America and Western Europe.

Receiving side, United States: the US Jewish population grew from about 250,000 in 1880 to over 3 million by the early 1920s; New York became the largest Jewish city in the world. The Hebrew Immigrant Aid Society (HIAS, founded 1881) met the ships in New York. More than 40,000 of the Russian departures went to the Land of Israel in this period. The German-language American press — the papers the immigrants read on arrival — covered the exodus as it happened: Chronicling America's German-language holdings for 1880–1914 alone run to 63,538 pages.

Sources: Library of Congress Country Studies — Israel · MyJewishLearning — Jewish Emigration in the 19th Century · YIVO — Leaving Mother Russia

1889–1924 — Baron Hirsch's money: Russia to Argentina

The first transport organized itself. On August 14, 1889, the steamship Weser docked at Buenos Aires carrying Russian Jews from Kamenetz-Podolsk in Podolia fleeing the pogroms. The sources give the party's size slightly differently — 824 (Jewish Virtual Library), 820 (Encyclopaedia Judaica), 813 in 120 families (from the passenger lists) — shown as a range because the sources differ. About 40 of the families bought land near the Palacios railway station in Santa Fe province and founded Moïseville (Moisés Ville) in 1889, before any Hirsch organization existed.

Then the money. In 1891 Baron Maurice de Hirsch founded the Jewish Colonization Association (JCA) in London (£2,000,000 capital, £7,000,000 more added in 1892) and, separately, the Baron de Hirsch Fund in the United States with $2,500,000. Committees in Russia selected colonist families; the JCA bought land in bulk in Argentina (302,736 hectares by 1896; 586,473 by 1914), organized and subsidized the transports, and settled each family on a farm of about 185 acres bought on long-term credit. Hirsch said in an 1892 interview (People's Voice, Wellington, Kan., Sept. 23, 1892): he had “sent 6,000 Jews there” and negotiated for millions of acres. The German-language American press reported the scheme from its first months — “Baron Hirsch / Argentinien” matches 52 pages in Chronicling America's German papers for 1891–1900, including Der Deutsche Correspondent (Baltimore), Sept. 11, 1891.

The numbers, sending claims against receiving counts: on the colonies at Hirsch's death in 1896, 910 families — 6,757 persons; settled on JCA land by the war era, 18,900 persons, peaking at 20,382 in 1925; moved under JCA auspices before 1914, about 25,000, with about 25,000 more coming on their own. Argentina's own counts: the 1895 census counted 6,085 Jews in the republic; the JCA's statistics count 118,213 Jewish immigrants entering Argentina in 1904–1924 alone; the Jewish population was an estimated 100,000–117,000 by 1914 and 125,000 by 1919. The failure side is in the record too: the New-York Tribune's front page of August 7, 1892 — “BARON HIRSCH'S COLONY A FAILURE.”

Sources: Baron Hirsch & the Argentina colonies — this site · Encyclopaedia Judaica — Argentina

1907–1914 — The Galveston Movement: Bremen to Galveston to the interior

Banker Jacob Schiff put up nearly $500,000 of his own money to divert Jewish immigrants away from crowded New York to the port of Galveston, Texas, and from there to the American interior. The Jewish Immigrants' Information Bureau ran the receiving end; the ships sailed from Bremen.

Both ends, with the counts. The first group arrived on the SS Cassel on July 1, 1907. A Federal Reserve study of the movement counts 54 program participants on that sailing; the Denver Jewish Outlook of August 23, 1907 reports from the dockside that among the 875 aliens aboard the Cassel were 86 Jews, “the first lot of Jewish immigrants to be diverted to a southern port from New York.” The two numbers count different things — program participants vs. all Jewish passengers — and both are kept. Year by year (Texas State Historical Association): 1907, about 900 before year's end; 1908, only 106; 1909, 773; 1910, 2,500; 1911, 1,400. The total, as the sources give it: about 10,000 Jewish immigrants from more than 7,000 families — 10,076 extracted from the Bremen departure lists; the Texas Historical Commission's marker gives the bureau's own count, 9,332. The range is shown rather than a single picked figure. From Galveston the arrivals were dispersed across the South, Midwest and West — the 1907 article names the method: a miller to a milling center, “a blacksmith to Denver or Kansas City.” The movement ended in 1914; Schiff had spent roughly half his pledge.

Sources: The Jewish Outlook, Aug. 23, 1907, p. 2 — Library of Congress · TSHA Handbook — Galveston Movement · Texas Historical Commission marker

1914–1918 — The First World War: expulsions and refugees in the East

When the front rolled across the Pale of Settlement and Galicia, the Russian high command treated the Jews of the war zone as enemy agents and expelled them eastward wholesale; on the Austrian side, Galician Jews fled west before the Russian advance.

Sending side (Russian Empire): in 1915 the Russian army expelled the Jews from the front provinces — 500,000–600,000 exiled to Russia's inner provinces, and about 100,000 more fled the war zones (Virtual Shtetl). The American Jewish Committee's 1916 report, written while it was happening, counted more: “no fewer than 800,000 have been driven from their homes… [those expelled and forced to flee] number 600,000 at the least.” Modern historians go higher still — roughly 500,000 expelled from the northwestern provinces alone, and about 1,000,000 displaced across Russia in 1914–15. The honest statement is a range: 500,000 to about 1,000,000. Named places: in Kovno province, all 40,000 Jews were ordered out in May 1915, given two days, and shipped “in box cars… to the distant governments of Poltava, Ekaterinoslav and Taurida” — sending province and receiving provinces both named.

Galicia (Austria-Hungary): about 400,000 Galician Jews fled their homes; 77,000 reached Vienna, with refugee camps at Nikolsburg, Pohrlitz and Gaya in Moravia and Bohemia, while Warsaw received about 80,000 displaced persons. The American Jewish Year Book's contemporary count for Galicia is lower — 200,000 fled — and is noted as differing. The relief machinery — the Joint Distribution Committee, founded 1914 — is the same organization that runs the orphan work in the next section.

Sources: Virtual Shtetl — The First World War · AJC — The Jews in the Eastern War Zone, 1916 (Gutenberg)

1919–1924 — War orphans to America; the search for the Poland article; the gates close

The verdict first, honestly. A specific pre-WWII newspaper article about Jews in Poland, parents alive, sending their children to the USA by choice was searched for hard — English papers, the Library of Congress, and the Yiddish press — and was not found. What the record does hold, in named papers with dates, pages and exact words, is the real traffic underneath the memory: in 1921, American Jewish newspapers repeatedly reported Polish Jewish children being sent to the United States — war and pogrom orphans, carried to relatives in America by the Joint Distribution Committee's War Orphans Bureau and HIAS. The documented parents-alive version of “sending the children to America” is the One Thousand Children program of 1934–1945, which brought roughly 1,000–1,400 mostly Jewish children from Germany and Austria — not Poland. The Kindertransport likewise ran from Germany, Austria and Czechoslovakia to Britain.

The verified 1921 articles (Detroit Jewish Chronicle, University of Michigan archive). August 5, 1921, p. 7: Roza Glichlich, age 7, of Warsaw, whose parents and five sisters died of typhus, sailed on the S.S. Lithuania to Boston and then to her uncle in Bayonne, New Jersey: “On that trip Roza had the companionship of 14 other war orphans, [sent] to welcoming relatives in America by the War Orphans' Bureau of the Joint Distribution Committee…” and “Of the 50,000 Jewish war orphans for whom the bureau hopes to find homes it has already tabulated 10,000…” September 16, 1921, p. 1: “Aboard the S. S. Lithuania, arriving at Brooklyn last week, was a little [party] of 18 war orphans, the youngest not quite 6… The children are all natives of Poland and have been brought here to be placed among relatives by the Joint Distribution Committee of New York.” September 30, 1921: how the system worked — each American relative deposited affidavits and “the necessary funds to cover all expenses, including ship ticket, visas, necessary clothing, board and lodging while awaiting embarkation”; the children were sheltered in a special JDC home in Warsaw, escorted to the port, and met by HIAS in America.

The archival frame: the JDC created the War Orphans Bureau in 1920; two orphans from Turów, near Minsk, whose father was already in New York, came on the S.S. Polonia, arriving New York in December 1921. The Bureau's records describe some 1,500 orphans from Soviet Russia placed abroad — the United States, Canada, South Africa and Palestine. The same traffic went to Canada (orphans assembled in Antwerp in August 1921, sailing for Canada) and to South Africa, where Isaac Ochberg brought 200 orphans from Polish Ukraine and Galicia to Cape Town in 1921.

The Yiddish press covered all of it. Chronicling America holds real Yiddish dailies (Der Tog, Der Morgen Zshurnal, the Yidishes Tageblatt). A Hebrew-script search for “orphans,” 1919–1925, returns 3,177 pages, including the Yidishes Tageblatt of August 5, 1921 — the very week of the Roza Glichlich story. A search for “Poland children,” 1919–1939, returns 43 pages, among them the Morgen Zshurnal of 1937–38 — pre-war candidate pages for the remembered article that have not yet been read one by one; that read is an open item, stated plainly. The National Library of Israel's Historical Jewish Press — the main archive of the Forverts and Der Tog — stayed blocked (403) on repeated tries; recorded as blocked, not as searched. The Emergency Quota Act of 1921 and the Immigration Act of 1924 then closed the gates: the era of mass Jewish immigration to the United States ended here.

Sources: Detroit Jewish Chronicle, Aug. 5, 1921, p. 7 · Detroit Jewish Chronicle, Sept. 16, 1921, p. 1 · JDC Archives — Coming to America · YIVO — One Thousand Children

1933–1939 — Out of Germany and Austria

The frame. Germany's June 1933 census counted 499,682 Jews by religion; with those counted as Jews by descent the figure usually given is about 523,000–525,000. Austria held about 185,000–192,000. What followed was counted year by year by the Reichsvertretung der Deutschen Juden and its successor:

YearJews who left Germany
193337,000
193423,000
193521,000
193625,000
193723,000
1938about 40,000 (one text table says 47,000 — the sources differ; both shown)
193968,000 (other counts run to 78,000)

Totals and destinations (both ends). By September 1939, the US Holocaust Memorial Museum counts about 282,000 Jews had left Germany; other estimates run to about 300,000–330,000, and the range is shown. From Austria, about 117,000 of 185,000 had left. Where they went (USHMM figures for the decade): about 95,000 to the United States, 60,000 to Palestine, 40,000 to Britain, about 75,000 to Central and South America, and more than 18,000 to Shanghai — the one port that asked no visa. Of the Jews who stayed in Germany, the October 1941 count was about 163,000; those who could not get out were deported east from October 1941.

Sources: USHMM — German Jewish Refugees, 1933–1939 · Wikipedia — Emigration of Jews from Nazi Germany

1938–1939 — Children to Britain; the ship nobody would take

Kindertransport. After Kristallnacht (November 9–10, 1938), Britain agreed to take unaccompanied Jewish children, no numbers limit, on a £50 bond per child. The first transport left Berlin on December 1, 1938 and arrived at Harwich on December 2 — about 200 children from a Berlin Jewish orphanage burned in the pogrom night. Trains and boats followed from Vienna, Prague, Danzig, Hamburg, Frankfurt and Cologne, most landing at Harwich and Liverpool Street Station, London. In all, about 10,000 children reached Britain before the war stopped the transports. Nicholas Winton's trains brought 669 children from Czechoslovakia.

The St. Louis — the movement refused. On May 13, 1939, the MS St. Louis left Hamburg for Havana with 937 passengers, nearly all Jewish refugees holding Cuban landing permits that Cuba then invalidated. Cuba admitted 28; the United States and Canada refused the ship; it docked back at Antwerp on June 17, 1939. The passengers were divided among four receiving countries: 288 to Britain, 181 to the Netherlands, 214 to Belgium, 224 to France. Of those landed on the continent, 254 were later killed in the Holocaust (USHMM; Britannica gives 255 — both shown).

Sources: USHMM — Kindertransport · Britannica — St. Louis

1945–1948 — The DP camps and the Bricha

The frame. Europe's Jews numbered about 9.5 million in 1933 and about 3.5 million in 1950. At the surrender in May 1945, only about 55,000–60,000 Jews were among the displaced persons in Germany and Austria; the camps then filled with survivors and with Jews fleeing renewed violence in Poland.

In all, more than 250,000 Jewish displaced persons passed through or lived in the DP camps and communities of Germany, Austria and Italy between 1945 and 1952. The Bricha (“flight”), the underground movement that moved survivors from Eastern Europe to the DP camps and on to Mediterranean ports for Palestine, transferred about 250,000 Jews between 1944 and 1948 — about 170,000 of them Polish Jews moving to Austria, Germany and Italy. The trigger for the largest wave: the Kielce pogrom of July 4, 1946 (42 Jews killed) — from July to August 1946 about 73,000 Jews left Poland; other counts put the post-Kielce flight at 90,000–100,000 over the following months, and both are shown. The ships were stopped at Cyprus: more than 50,000 refugees were interned in British detention camps there between 1946 and 1949. Where the DPs finally went: about 136,000 to Israel after May 1948, about 80,000 to the United States under the Displaced Persons Acts, and about 20,000 to other countries.

Sources: Wikipedia — Bricha · USHMM — Jewish Displaced Persons

1948–1951 — A state doubles itself; the airlifts from Yemen and Iraq

The frame. In May 1948 the new State of Israel held about 650,000 Jews. In three and a half years 687,000 immigrants arrived, and by the end of 1951 the Jewish population had doubled to about 1,300,000. The peak year was 1949: 239,954 arrivals.

Operation Magic Carpet — Yemen and Aden to Israel. Between June 1949 and September 1950, 380 flights flew out of Aden. The Encyclopaedia Judaica's count: 48,315 Yemenite and Adeni Jews airlifted; the operation's total is usually rounded to about 49,000, including some 400 from Djibouti and Asmara and about 1,700 from Aden itself. The passengers had walked from across Yemen to the camp the Joint Distribution Committee ran outside Aden. Yemen's ancient Jewish community — about 50,000–63,000 people in 1948, the counts differ — was reduced to a remnant of about 2,000.

Operation Ezra and Nehemiah — Iraq to Israel. In March 1950 Iraq passed a law letting Jews leave if they renounced their citizenship and their property. The airlift ran from Baghdad — with a refueling stop in Cyprus — to Lod airport. The Encyclopaedia Judaica's count: 123,370 Iraqi Jews airlifted in 1950–51; the figure most often quoted is about 120,000. A second scholarly count puts the direct Baghdad–Lod airlift at “over 112,000” — the difference is the counting frame (registered emigrants vs. airlift passengers), and both are shown. Iraq's Jewish community, some 2,600 years old and numbering roughly 135,000–160,000 in the late 1940s (counts differ), was left with a few thousand.

Sources: Encyclopaedia Judaica — Operation Magic Carpet · Wikipedia — Operation Ezra and Nehemiah

1961–1964 — Morocco: Operation Yachin

After Moroccan independence, emigration was restricted and Jews left secretly; after the sinking of the clandestine ship Egoz on January 10–11, 1961 — 46 drowned — a negotiated, semi-official operation replaced the secret boats. In Operation Yachin (November 1961 to spring 1964), HIAS organized the departure: Jews traveled from Casablanca and Tangier by ship and plane, most routed through France and Italy, to Israel. The reported arrangement: HIAS paid the Moroccan government a per-capita fee — reported figures are an initial $500,000 and $100 for each of the first 10,000 emigrants and $250 a head after that (flagged here as reported, not ledger-verified).

The numbers, both ends: 90,000–97,000 Moroccan Jews reached Israel under Yachin (the sources give both endpoints). Morocco's Jewish population was counted at 162,420 in early 1961 and 53,000 by 1967 — the receiving and sending sides of the same exodus. The earlier organized wave, run by the Jewish Agency's Cadima (1949–1956), had already taken roughly 60,000.

Sources: Wikipedia — Operation Yachin · JIMENA — The Egoz

1971–1991 — Soviet Jewry: the exit-visa years

After 1967 a movement of Soviet Jews demanded exit visas for Israel; the USSR let out a trickle, then a stream, then shut it down, then — under perestroika — opened the gates. The counting frame matters: exit visas were issued for Israel; many emigrants changed destination in Vienna, the transit point, and went to the United States instead.

The numbers. 1970s total: more than 250,000 Soviet Jews left in 1971–1980. Peak year 1979: 51,320 exit visas — but by then only about a third went to Israel (17,614 Israel arrivals in 1979), the rest to the US. Trough: 1984, just 894. Overall for 1970–1988: 291,000 exit visas — 165,000 to Israel, 126,000 to the United States. On the receiving side: the transit camp at Schönau, Austria, and Jewish Agency and HIAS processing in Vienna and Rome.

Sources: Wikipedia — 1970s Soviet Union aliyah · Jewish Virtual Library — Soviet Jewry

1984–2006 — Ethiopia, and the post-Soviet million

Operation Moses (1984–85). Ethiopian Jews (Beta Israel) walked from Gondar and Tigray to refugee camps in Sudan; from November 21, 1984 to January 5, 1985, a secret airlift via Brussels carried about 8,000 of them from Khartoum to Israel. Of about 15,000 who set out on foot, some 4,000 died of disease, hunger and attacks along the way. When the airlift leaked, it stopped; Operation Joshua (March 1985) brought about 650 more from Sudan with US help.

Operation Solomon (1991). With Addis Ababa about to fall in the civil war, Israel negotiated the release of the remaining community. In about 36 hours, May 24–25, 1991, 41 aircraft flew 14,325 Ethiopian Jews (some sources give 14,324 — the one-person difference is in the sources, shown not hidden) from Addis Ababa to Israel; one El Al 747 carried 1,122 passengers, a world record.

The post-Soviet wave (1989–2006). When the USSR opened emigration and then dissolved: about 1.6 million Jews and their family members left the former Soviet Union — about 979,000 to Israel, 325,000 to the United States, 219,000 to Germany. The peak: 1990, when about 228,400 left and 185,227 of them arrived in Israel; in 1991, about 148,000 arrived in Israel. In 1989 itself, 71,000 had left but only 12,117 went to Israel — the last year of the old pattern before the gates opened fully.

Sources: Wikipedia — Operation Solomon · Jewish Federation of Greater Portland — Operation Moses
